messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Weakness Belief: I am a weak person

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Layla, a 77-year-old Middle Eastern woman who had lived alone for many years and worked part-time as a tutor, described her trauma as the period when shelling and street fighting pushed ordinary life into a state of constant danger. She spoke of the day she was caught outdoors while moving between her apartment and a nearby shop, when the noise seemed to arrive from nowhere and the street around her changed in an instant. What she remembered most was the shock of not knowing where to go, the fear in her body, and the desperate need to get inside somewhere with a door she could shut. In the months that followed, after the violence in her area became an inescapable part of daily life, Layla began to organize everything around safety in a way that felt necessary to her. Even now, when she tutors, she automatically chooses a seat nearest the classroom or office exit, not because she expects anything specific to happen in that room, but because being able to leave quickly has become the one thing that helps her feel she is not trapped. If a room has only one obvious way out or if she is asked to sit deeper inside, she becomes tense and watches the door.

Over time, Layla noticed that anything resembling the events of that period could bring her straight back to it without warning. A sudden bang from the street, the sharp crack of a dropped object, or a moment of commotion in the building where she teaches can instantly pull the whole memory forward, not as a distant recollection but as if the same scene has opened again around her. When this happens, she is not simply reminded of what she went through; she feels the terror from then return at full strength. She described it as “the same fear in my chest,” and said that when she remembers the frightening day, it is not like telling herself a story about the past. Instead, the event comes with such force that she feels as though it is happening right now, with the same urgency and helplessness. At those moments, she becomes acutely aware of sounds, movements, and exits around her, scanning the environment for anything that might signal danger.

Layla has tried to keep herself away from reminders whenever possible. She no longer watches television programmes or films that include war, explosions, displaced families, or similar suffering, and she avoids reading news or articles that describe events like the one she lived through. She has come to think that if she lets herself look at such material, she will be pulled too far back into it and will not be able to manage the feelings that follow. She said that even the idea of deliberately thinking about what happened makes her feel she would lose control over herself, so she pushes those thoughts away as soon as they appear. In her own mind, she has framed this as a test of endurance she does not trust herself to pass. She worries that if she stays with the memory, she will not be able to handle it and will be overwhelmed by it.

There is also a quieter loss she speaks about with sadness: she dwells on how she used to be before the event. Layla remembers herself as more settled, more willing to move freely through the city, and more engaged with the daily routines that once gave her life shape. She now compares that person with who she feels she has become and sees someone diminished. She said she feels “dead inside,” a phrase she used without drama, as though naming an emotional fact she has grown used to living with. That numbness has made her feel distant from the woman she believes she was before the violence, and it leaves her grieving not only what happened, but who she thinks she lost in the process.

Layla’s tutoring work has continued, but it now takes more effort to sustain than it once did. She still meets students, yet she chooses rooms carefully, sits near the exit, and remains alert to any sudden noise in the corridor or street outside. She knows these habits may look small to other people, but to her they are what make it possible to keep going. Even so, the need to arrange her surroundings this way has narrowed her life. She has declined invitations to watch films with others and often avoids conversations that might lead to discussion of conflict or current events. What finally brought her to seek help was the sense that the past was appearing too easily in the present and that she was becoming increasingly frightened by her own reactions. She came hoping for relief from the moments when a sound or scene can seize her without warning, and fearing that if nothing changes she will remain trapped between the memory and the life she is trying to preserve.
